newsitem.title: UK: Mothers aware they have HIV can spare babies - study.
newsitem.headline: Mothers aware they have HIV can spare babies - study.

text.p: Pregnant women infected with the HIV virus that causes AIDS will take action to spare their babies -- if they know they are infected, British and Irish doctors reported on Thursday.

The study showed those who were told of the risks were 15 times less likely to breastfeed their babies than most mothers. Seventy-five percent took drugs aimed at reducing mother-to-child transmission.
Several studies have shown that taking anti-viral drugs can help prevent transmission of the deadly virus from mother to child, as can avoiding breast-feeding.
The HIV virus is spread through body fluids.

The study, coordinated by Dr Diana Gibb at London's Institute of Child Health and the Royal College of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, involved all reports of HIV-positive pregnant women in Britain and Ireland.

"Between 1990 and 1995 inclusive, based on anonymous unlinked testing of neonatal bloods, it can be estimated that at least 1,274 children were born to HIV-infected women in the UK and Ireland," the researchers wrote in a report in the journal AIDS.
Surveys showed most of the mothers were infected abroad -- many in Africa, where AIDS has reached epidemic proportions in many countries.

The researchers found that 44 percent of HIV-infected mothers who knew of their condition chose to deliver their babies by Caesarean section, which can reduce the risk of transmission. Only four percent of those who knew have chosen to breast-feed since 1990.
But the researchers complained that most HIV-positive women did not know they had the virus. In London in 1995, only 18 percent of pregnant women with HIV were diagnosed.
"The majority of infected pregnant women, particularly in London, are of African origin, have high rates of breastfeeding and remain unaware of their diagnosis," they wrote.

"If all pregnant women in London were aware of their infection status and took up interventions at the rates seen in the study, the number of infected babies each year in London could be reduced from an estimated 41 to 13."
